title: Counting sort
short: Sort small whole numbers by counting them, no comparing.
what: When values are small whole numbers, make one counter per possible value. Read the list once and add 1 to each value's counter. Then walk the counters in order and write each value as many times as it was counted.
analogy: Sorting coins. You don't compare coins with each other: you drop each one into its tray (1c, 5c, 10c), then empty the trays in order.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: Values go from 0 to 4, so make 5 counters, all 0. The index under each box is the value it counts.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: Read 3, 1, 4: add 1 to count[3], count[1] and count[4]. No comparisons at all.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: Read 1, 0, 3, 1. Now the counts say: one 0, three 1s, no 2s, two 3s, one 4.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: Walk the counters left to right and write each value count times. count[0] is 1: write one 0.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: count[1] is 3: write 1 three times. count[2] is 0: write nothing.

frames.label: input: 3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1
frames.say: Then two 3s and one 4. Sorted after one pass over the input and one pass over 5 counters: O(n + k).

when: Values are whole numbers in a small range
You need faster than O(n log n)
python:
def counting_sort(nums, max_value):
    count = [0] * (max_value + 1)
    for x in nums:
        count[x] += 1
    out = []
    for value, times in enumerate(count):
        out.extend([value] * times)
    return count, out

count, out = counting_sort([3, 1, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1], 4)
print(count)
print(out)
cost: Sort n values from 0 to k
watch: k is the size of the range, not the number of items. Values up to 10**9 need 10**9 counters.
Negative values need an offset: count[x - smallest].
For a few values, collections.Counter(nums) does the counting.
